questions.stem: A monitoring script takes the terminal ID from every 1987 ASCII request at a fixed character position, measured on requests from the first terminal model. A second model's requests also carry field 14, the card's expiry date. What does the script report for the second model?

options.text: The correct terminal ID, since the bitmap tells the script where field 41 begins
options.says: Section 1.1: the bitmap only says which fields are present; a reader that uses a fixed offset never reads it, and finding field 41 means walking every field before it.

options.text: The correct terminal ID, since each field number has a reserved place in the message
options.says: Section 1.1: only the fields whose bit is set travel, so no field has a fixed position; adding field 22 moved field 41 from offset 72 to 75.

options.text: Text from the wrong place, since field 14 moves every later field along by its length
options.says: Section 1.1: fields follow in field-number order, so a field added before 41 moves it; the page's fixed-offset reader then reads the wrong terminal.

options.text: Text from the wrong place, since field 14 moves the bitmap away from the start
options.says: Section 1.1: the bitmap always follows the MTI; adding field 22 changed a bit in it and moved field 41, not the bitmap.

origin.section: 1.1. A Message Is an MTI, a Bitmap and the Fields the Bitmap Announces

questions.stem: Two processors both name ISO 8583:1987 in their specifications. The first writes each digit as an ASCII character; the second packs two digits into a byte. A client built for the first sends its first purchase to the second. What happens?

options.text: The host reads it correctly, since both links follow the same edition of the standard
options.says: Section 1.2: the standard fixes what a field means, not how its digits are written; the same 0100 packed for one 1987 packager could not be read by the other.

options.text: The host reads it correctly, since the bitmap tells the host how each field is encoded
options.says: Section 1.1 and 1.2: the bitmap says which fields are present; the encoding comes from each side's field definitions, the network's dialect.

options.text: The host cannot read it, since the edition fixes what fields mean but not their bytes
options.says: Section 1.2: the encoding belongs to each network's dialect; the iso87ascii and iso87binary messages failed to unpack with each other's packager.

options.text: The host cannot read it, since the 1987 edition forbids ASCII digits between hosts
options.says: Section 1.2: ASCII, BCD, binary and EBCDIC are all choices a dialect makes; jPOS ships a 1987 packager for ASCII as well as binary.

origin.section: 1.2. The Standard Fixes What a Field Means, and Each Link Fixes Its Bytes

questions.stem: A network moves from a 1987 dialect to a 1993 one. The acquirer's client gets the new packager, but its code still treats a response as approved only when field 39 equals "00". A purchase of 64.20 comes back with 000 in field 39. What does the cardholder experience?

options.text: The till shows a decline, while the issuer has approved and taken or held the amount
options.says: Section 1.3: 000 in field 39 is a 1993 approval, so the client reports a decline while the issuer has approved and holds the funds, and no reversal goes out.

options.text: The till shows a decline, while the issuer has declined and moved no money
options.says: Section 1.3: 000 is a 1993 approval, so the issuer approved; only the client's check is wrong, and the funds are held while the cardholder hears "declined".

options.text: The till shows an approval, since 000 begins with the two digits the client expects
options.says: Section 1.3: the check is equality with "00", and "00".equals("000") printed false.

options.text: The till shows an approval, since the new packager shortens 000 to 00 when it reads
options.says: Section 1.3: the 1993 packager read field 39 as 000; nothing converts it to the 1987 form.

origin.section: 1.3. The First MTI Digit Names the Edition, and Editions Disagree on Fields

questions.stem: A switch company changes one of jPOS's classes in its own copy of the source, builds the jar, and runs it as a service that partner banks' systems connect to over the internet. It never gives the jar or its code to anyone. What does the AGPL v3 mean for it?

options.text: It owes no one the source, since it never distributes a copy of the software
options.says: Section 1.4: that is the GPL's trigger; the AGPL's section 13 adds an obligation toward users of a modified version over a network.

options.text: It owes no one the source, since it changed only one class of the library
options.says: Section 1.4: the obligation follows any modified version; the page's processor patched a single channel class.

options.text: It may owe the banks the source, since they interact with its version over a network
options.says: Section 1.4: if you modify the program and users interact with your version over a network, you must offer them its source; the connecting systems may be such users.

options.text: It may owe the banks the source, since any paid service built on jPOS must publish it
options.says: Section 1.4: the obligation starts with modifying the program, not with charging for a service; a commercial licence exists for those who can't meet the terms.

origin.section: 1.4. jPOS Is AGPL: Network Users of Your Modified Version Are Offered Its Source
